newsitem.title: UK: Howard's UK Conservative leadership bid torpedoed.
newsitem.headline: Howard's UK Conservative leadership bid torpedoed.

text.p: Former Interior Minister Michael Howard's bid to be Britain's next Conservative Party leader has been stopped in its tracks by his embittered ex-deputy.

Less than three weeks after the Conservatives suffered their worst election defeat for 150 years, the new parliament was treated to the unedifying spectacle of defeated ministers trading bitter blows.
Howard sat stony-faced in the House of Commons on Monday as former prisons minister Ann Widdecombe acccused him of misleading parliament after sacking the head of the prison service in 1995.
Oozing contempt, she accused her former boss of being "a man whose reaction to attack is denial and semantic prestidigitation".
Howard then icily refuted her vitriolic attack, telling lawmakers: "At no time did I cross the line between what I was entitled to do and what I wasn't."
Widdecombe accused Howard of in effect overruling the former head of the prison service and ordering suspension of the governor of Parkhurst prison in southern England after a major break-out.
In the election on May 1, voters deserted the Conservatives en masse, angered that their 18 years in power had ended in scandal and division.
Politicians battling to rebuild the demoralised Conservatives had hoped to heal the wounds after years of party in-fighting.

But the public grudge match between Widdecombe and Howard put paid to any fragile hopes of restoring unity in the near future and several Conservatives felt Howard's leadership chances had been dealt a mortal blow.
The Conservatives, who once boasted they were the finest election-winning machine in the world, have been reduced to a dispirited rump of 164 members in the 659-seat chamber.
For Labour, rejuvenated and tightly disciplined by their leader Tony Blair, swept to the biggest election victory in its history and are now set for five years in power to transform Britain.
Howard has laid down a hard-line position on Europe, eager to win the backing of Eurosceptic Conservatives who fear Brussels is plotting to set up a United States of Europe.
At the other end of the political spectrum is former finance minister Kenneth Clarke, a fervent pro-European and powerful parliamentary performer.
But much of the media spotlight has centred on the 36-year-old former Welsh Secretary William Hague.
Bookmakers make him the odds-on favourite even if Hague is perhaps best known for a storming speech he made to the Conservative Party conference when just 16 years old.
But with the blood-letting now carrying on beyond the election, the winner of the contest could be claiming a poisoned chalice when the 164 Conservative lawmakers pick their new leader this summer.
